definition.text: Catch per unit effort (CPUE) is an indirect measure of how abundant a target species is, based on how much is caught for a given amount of fishing.

facts.text: A falling CPUE signals overexploitation, while a steady CPUE signals sustainable harvesting.
It does not disrupt normal harvesting and is easy to collect and analyse, so harvesters themselves can use it.
The main difficulty is defining the unit of effort, and CPUE is often not linearly related to abundance.

definition.text: Density dependence is when a population's growth rate is controlled by how crowded the population is.

facts.text: In negative density dependence, crowding, predators and competition slow growth; each individual leaves fewer offspring.
In positive density dependence, or the Allee effect, growth speeds up as density rises.
Fish populations can be harvested sustainably because thinning them out raises growth, the density-dependent response.

definition.text: Discards are the part of a catch that is not kept on board but thrown back into the sea, often dead or dying.

facts.text: Fish are discarded for economic and political reasons: they are unmarketable, below minimum landing size, or over quota.
Discards are part of bycatch; highgrading, dumping marketable fish to make room for more valuable ones, also causes them.
North Sea discards were estimated at 800,000–950,000 tonnes a year, about one-third of the weight landed.
Survival varies by species and gear, from 88 to 98 per cent for some flatfish and sharks to much lower for roundfish.

definition.text: A discard ban requires fishers to land what they catch, so that dead discards are counted in the fishing mortality used for management.

facts.text: Norway banned discarding some commercial species in 1987, combined with monitoring and closing areas when bycatch gets too high.
In New Zealand, discarding rose right after ITQs began, until the government raised payment for over-quota landings from 10 to 50 per cent of market price.
Older EU quota rules forced fishers to discard over-quota fish; the reformed Common Fisheries Policy added a Landing Obligation.

title: Exclusive economic zone

definition.text: An exclusive economic zone (EEZ) is a sea area, set by the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, where a coastal state has exclusive rights to explore and use marine resources.

facts.text: It runs from the edge of territorial waters at 12 nautical miles to 200 nautical miles from the coast.
Territorial waters once extended only 3 nautical miles, the range of a cannon shot.
EEZ boundaries are a common source of conflict; the UK–Iceland Cod Wars ended with a 1976 agreement.
Fish stocks that cross EEZ boundaries, transboundary stocks, are a key concept in controlling them.
Beyond EEZs fishing is hard to control, and most high-seas fisheries survive only on subsidies.
About one-third of the ocean lies within EEZs.
